title: All of life rests on trust
source_text: Εἴπερ οὖν δεῖ πιστεύειν, ὡς ὁ λόγος ἐδίδαξεν. ἑνί τινι τῶν αἱρέσεις εἰσηγησαμένων ἐν Ἕλλησιν ἢ βαρβάροις. πῶς οὐχὶ μᾶλλον τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ καὶ τῷ διδάσκοντι τοῦτον μόνον δεῖν σέβειν τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ, ἤτοι ὡς μὴ ὄντα ἢ ὡς ὄντα μὲν καὶ τιμῆς ἄξια οὐ μὴν καὶ προσκυνήσεως καὶ σεβασμοῦ, παρορᾶν; περὶ ὧν ὁ μὴ πιστεύων μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ λόγῳ θεωρῶν τὰ πράγματα ἐρεῖ τὰς ὑποπιπτούσας αὐτῷ καὶ εὑρισκομένας ἐκ τοῦ πάνυ ζητεῖν ἀποδείξεις. πῶς δ᾿ οὐκ εὐλογώτερον, πάντων τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων πίστεως ἠρτημένων. ἐκείνων μᾶλλον πιστεύειν τῷ θεῷ; τίς γὰρ πλεῖ ἢ γαμεῖ ἢ παιδοποιεῖται ἢ ῥίπτει τὰ σπέρματα ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν μὴ τὰ κρείττονα πιστεύων ἀπαντήσεσθαι. δυνατοῦ ὄντος καὶ τοῦ ἐναντία γενέσθαι καὶ ἔστιν ὅτε γινομένου; ἀλλ᾿ ὅμως ἡ περὶ τοῦ τὰ κρείττονα καὶ τὰ κατ᾿ εὐχὴν ἀπαντήσεσθαι πίστις τολμᾶν πάντας ποιεῖ καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ ἄδηλα καὶ δυνατὰ ἄλλως συμβῆναι. εἰ δὲ συνέχει τὸν βίον ἐν πάσῃ πράξει ἀδήλῳ, ὅπως ἐκβήσεται. ἡ ἐλπὶς καὶ ἡ περὶ τῶν μελλόντων χρηστοτέρα πίστις, πῶς οὐ μᾶλλον αὕτη παραληφθήσεται εὐλόγως τῷ πιστεύοντι ὑπὲρ τὴν πλεομένην θάλασσαν καὶ γῆν σπειρομένην καὶ γυναῖκα γαμουμένην καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ἐν ἀνθρώποις πράγματα τῷ ταῦτα πάντα δημιουργήσαντι θεῷ καὶ τῷ μετὰ ὑπερβαλλούσης μεγαλονοίας καὶ θείας μεγαλοφροσύνης τολμήσαντι τοῦτον τὸν λόγον παραστῆσαι τοῖς πανταχοῦ τῆς οἰκουμένης μετὰ μεγάλων κινδύνων καὶ θανάτου νομιζομένου ἀτίμου, ἃ ὑπέμεινεν ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων, διδάξας καὶ τοὺς ὑπηρετεῖσθαι τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ αὐτοῦ ἐν τῇ ἀρχῇ πεισθέντας μετὰ πάντων κινδύνων καὶ τῶν ἀεὶ προσδοκωμένων θανάτων τολμῆσαι ἀποδημῆσαι πανταχοῦ τῆς οἰκουμένης ὑπὲρ τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων σωτηρίας;
pass_a_gloss: If then one must believe (δεῖ πιστεύειν), as the argument (ὁ λόγος) taught, some one of those who introduced schools (αἱρέσεις εἰσηγησαμένων) among Greeks or barbarians, how not rather the God over all (τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ) and the one teaching that this one alone must be worshipped (σέβειν), and the rest, either as not being or as being and worthy of honour (τιμῆς ἄξια) but not of obeisance (προσκύνησις) and reverence (σεβασμός), to overlook (παρορᾶν)? About which the one not only believing but also contemplating (θεωρῶν) matters with reason (λόγῳ) will state the demonstrations (ἀποδείξεις) falling to him and found from searching (ζητεῖν) thoroughly. And how not more reasonable (εὐλογώτερον), all human things hanging on faith (πίστεως ἠρτημένων), to believe God rather than those? For who sails or marries or begets children or throws seeds on the earth not believing that the better things will meet him (ἀπαντήσεσθαι), it being possible also for the opposite to happen and sometimes happening? But nevertheless the faith about the better things and those according to prayer (κατ᾿ εὐχήν) coming makes all dare (τολμᾶν) even to the unclear things (ἄδηλα) and things possible to fall out otherwise. And if hope (ἐλπίς) and the kindlier faith (χρηστοτέρα πίστις) about things to come hold together (συνέχει) life in every action unclear as to how it will turn out, how will not this rather be taken up reasonably by the one believing — above (ὑπέρ) the sea sailed and earth sown and wife married and the rest of human affairs — the God who fashioned (δημιουργήσαντι) all these, and the one who with surpassing greatness of mind (μεγαλόνοια) and divine magnanimity (θεία μεγαλοφροσύνη) dared to present this word/teaching (τὸν λόγον) to those everywhere in the inhabited world (οἰκουμένη) with great dangers and a death considered dishonourable (θανάτου νομιζομένου ἀτίμου), which he endured for men (ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων), having taught also those persuaded in the beginning to serve (ὑπηρετεῖσθαι) his teaching (διδασκαλία) to dare, with all dangers and the deaths always expected, to travel abroad (ἀποδημῆσαι) everywhere in the world for the salvation (σωτηρία) of men?
pass_b_english: If, then, as our argument has shown, one must believe some one of those who founded schools among Greeks or barbarians, how much more must one believe the God who is over all, and the one who teaches that he alone must be worshipped, and that all else must be disregarded, either as not existing, or as existing and worthy of honour, yet not of adoration and worship? On these matters, the one who does not only believe but also contemplates things by reason will set out the proofs that occur to him and that he finds by diligent searching.

And since all human affairs depend on faith, how is it not more reasonable to believe God rather than those men? For who sails, or marries, or has children, or casts seed upon the ground, without believing that things will turn out for the better, though the opposite may happen and sometimes does? Yet the belief that things will turn out for the better and as one prays makes everyone venture even on what is uncertain and might fall out otherwise. And if hope, and the more hopeful belief about the future, holds life together in every action whose outcome is uncertain, how much more reasonably will this faith be embraced by one who trusts, more than in the sea that is sailed, the earth that is sown, the wife who is married and the other affairs of human life, in the God who made all these things? And how much more in him who, with surpassing greatness of mind and divine magnanimity, dared to set this teaching before people in every part of the world, amid great dangers and a death thought shameful, all of which he endured for humankind; and who taught also those first persuaded to serve his teaching to dare, amid every danger and the deaths they always expected, to go abroad into every part of the world for the salvation of human beings?

choices.choice: ‘The one who teaches’ (τῷ διδάσκοντι) and ‘him who … dared’ (τῷ … τολμήσαντι) are unnamed in the Greek but plainly mean Jesus; the English keeps them unnamed. πίστις is rendered ‘faith’ where Origen speaks of Christian faith and ‘belief’ for the everyday trust of sailors and farmers, to keep the argument clear; the Greek uses one word throughout. ὑπὲρ τὴν πλεομένην θάλασσαν taken as ‘more than in the sea that is sailed’. The relative ἅ (‘which he endured’) is plural and covers both the dangers and the death, hence ‘all of which’. The one long closing question is split into two questions in English without changing the content. Possible echoes, not cited inline: the shameful death (compare Hebrews 12:2) and the sending of the apostles into the whole world (compare Matthew 28:19); neither is quoted.
